title: People are a thicket
hookLine: an elephant trainer says animals are easy to read, people a tangle
last: GET OUT, MARA — I SEE YOU.

cards: Dog people will tell you a dog can't lie. When it's happy, the whole back half wags. When it's guilty, it can't meet your eyes.
People are harder. A smile can mean anything. A yes can mean no.
A fine can mean please ask again. A son of an elephant trainer named Pessa once sat with the Buddha and said exactly this, from long experience with animals much bigger than dogs.

teach.h: PEOPLE ARE A TANGLE; ANIMALS ARE OPEN
teach.b: This is the fifty-first discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, named for Kandaraka, a wanderer who came along with Pessa. Pessa says something honest. People are a tangle, a thicket.
Animals are an open clearing. I can train an elephant, he says, and in the time it takes to go to the town and back, it will show me every trick and dodge it has.

teach.h: BODY, WORDS AND MIND DON'T MATCH
teach.b: But the people who work in my house do one thing with their bodies, say another with their words, and have something else again in their minds. The Buddha agrees: that's so, Pessa. People are a thicket.
Then he offers a way through the tangle, not by reading faces, but by watching what people do to themselves and to others.

teach.h: FOUR KINDS: WHO DO THEY TORMENT?
teach.b: There are four kinds of people. One torments himself, with harsh practices that hurt only his own body. One torments others: the hunter, the butcher, the jailer, the one whose living is other people's pain.
One torments both: a king, say, who holds a great sacrifice that exhausts himself and drives his servants with sticks and fear.

And one torments neither, and lives, here and now, cool and at peace. Pessa is delighted, and leaves early, with somewhere to be. If he had stayed a little longer, the Buddha says, he would have gained a great deal.

Pessa's problem is everyone's: people are hard to read. But the answer isn't to become a better mind reader. It's to look at the harm and the ease people bring, and to ask which of the four you're becoming yourself.

how: Buddhist teachers use MN 51's four kinds of persons to reflect on harm and harmlessness, and to point to the person who torments neither self nor others as the ideal of the path.

o: a thicket, a tangle hard to see into
an open clearing in the forest

games.q: the four kinds of people — tap the pairs.
p: harsh practices on his own body
a living made from others' pain
the king exhausting himself and servants
cool and at peace, here and now

s: Pessa says animals are harder to read than people
he says animals are an open clearing, and people a thicket.
the Buddha agreed that people are a thicket
he agreed, then gave four kinds of people to look at instead of faces.
Pessa stayed to hear the whole teaching
he left early; the Buddha said he would have gained a great deal by staying.

games.q: you're Pessa. the Buddha has begun describing four kinds of people, and you're delighted. but you have somewhere to be. what happens in the story?
o: he asks to become a monk.
games.why: Pessa leaves early. after he goes, the Buddha tells the monks that if Pessa had stayed a little longer, he would have gained a great deal.

practice: Think of someone who confuses you, whose words don't match what they do, and don't try to solve them.
Ask the Buddha's question softly, where is the pain in their life, toward themselves, toward others, and let some compassion for the tangle come up.
Turn the question once toward yourself, without blame, then rest with the breath, open as a clearing.

wordCard.voice: Gahana. A thicket, a tangle: an elephant trainer's son's honest word for people, and the Buddha agreed.

orig.note: Pali gahana: a thicket, a tangle. people, Pessa says, are gahana.

carryVoice: Your line: people are thickets. Elephants are open; people take a little more patience. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 51, Kandaraka Sutta (the discourse to Kandaraka)
